groups.label: Which kit
groups.tradeoff: The street Complete Kit is $22,990 and every Coupe-R body piece is an option on it. The Coupe-R ($24,990) buys a competition cage, 750/500 lb springs and a fixed race seat, which are the parts a street car does not want.

groups.label: Engine & transmission
groups.tradeoff: BluePrint 347 EFI is the turnkey path with a hydraulic clutch bearing in the box, about $4,500 less than a Coyote package and better footroom at 6'2". The Coyote is the majority Gen 3 choice and sounds the part, but needs different mounts, headers, PS and A/C kits and a tighter footbox. Carb saves $2,200 and gives up cold starts.

groups.label: Front brakes
groups.tradeoff: Wilwood 12.88" ($2,000–2,300) is the near-universal street upgrade and needs 17"+ wheels. The standard 11" PBR brakes are adequate and the only choice with 15s. Levy's 14" kit is for 18"+ wheels and track use.

groups.label: Rear suspension
groups.tradeoff: IRS rides and tracks better and is what nearly every street Gen 3 runs; it costs roughly $3,000 more than the 3-link once you add the center section and shocks. The 3-link is simpler, lighter and fine for a budget or track car, but you can't switch later.

groups.label: Rear brakes
groups.tradeoff: IRS 11.65"/13" keeps the OEM parking brake and costs the least; Wilwood 12.88" rears ($2,299) match the fronts visually and need an electric or MC4 parking brake solution.

groups.label: Differential
groups.tradeoff: The 2018 Mustang 3.55 unit from FFR is the no-donor path and what Ron L. runs. A Torsen ($775, diff only) adds traction for a street car but you still need the FFR carrier parts.

groups.label: Steering
groups.tradeoff: FFR's hydraulic kit (16799) needs a pump on the 347's front drive, which has to share with the A/C compressor; electric assist ($935) avoids that and the belt, at the cost of a less natural feel. Manual is cheapest and FFR warns you'll regret it.

groups.label: Steering wheel
groups.tradeoff: FFR's 14" wheel is included; a 13" Sparco gives more knee room but heavier steering on a manual rack. A quick-release hub helps entry more than any wheel choice.

groups.label: Clutch hydraulics
groups.tradeoff: 34158 ($220) is the only piece you need with the BluePrint package. Tilton and Forte's kits are for builds that don't come with a bearing.

groups.label: Headers
groups.tradeoff: FFR's 302 headers ($order form) are what the side pipes are designed around. GAS-N long-tubes ($1,095+) flow better and route more gracefully but have had months-long shipping delays.

groups.label: Side exhaust
groups.tradeoff: FFR stainless pipes ($1,525) are the default and loud (~114 dB inside). GAS-N Touring (from $1,495) is the quiet drop-in; Boig quieter still but call-to-order. Inserts ($120–160 a side) are the cheap fix for either.

groups.label: Fan & shroud
groups.tradeoff: Breeze 70807 ($99) is made for the FFR fan and this chassis; a SPAL swap buys little and loses the shroud fit.

groups.label: Battery
groups.tradeoff: Odyssey PC925 ($250) is the proven small AGM; Braille B2015 saves 13 lb for about the same money but is a race battery.

groups.label: Fuel system
groups.tradeoff: FFR's in-tank kit (17680, ~$600) is simplest and what most Sniper builders run; the Holley 12-345 module ($335) gives 3/8" lines and a proper bypass regulator for Sniper 2.

groups.label: Gauges
groups.tradeoff: FFR's GPS set ($1,299) is the coupe default and skips the TKX speed-sensor hassle. Speedhut custom is the same gauges with your choices; Dakota Digital is for a custom dash.

groups.label: A/C & heat
groups.tradeoff: FFR's 302/351W kit (~$1,800) is the only one that fits without fabrication; its weak point is defrost. FormaCars HVAC is the one proven alternative but has no public price. Decide before the footbox closes.

groups.label: Side windows
groups.tradeoff: FFR sliders ($549) are what nearly everyone runs and leak a little; FormaCars roll-downs are the Washington-rain answer, cost unknown, and must be done before door finishing.

groups.label: Wipers
groups.tradeoff: FFR's Lucas kit ($499) is marginal on the big windshield but fits; Specialty Power Windows ($376) sweeps better. Either is far easier with the body off.

groups.label: Mirrors
groups.tradeoff: FFR Raydots (included, extra for the pair) pass inspection; BRE's $289 coupe kit is the period-correct upgrade with backing plates.

groups.label: Seats
groups.tradeoff: FFR low-backs give the most headroom for the money; Kirkey ($250 + cover) is thinner still and floor-mounts. Corbeau and Sparco recline but cost headroom. Sit in a car before buying.

groups.label: Belts
groups.tradeoff: The included Simpson 5-point is track-correct; Schroth's ASM 4-point ($325) is the street-friendlier harness.

groups.label: Dash
groups.tradeoff: The aluminum dash is included; wrapping it over foam is the cheap upgrade; carbon ($600) is a look; a custom dash is a project.

groups.label: Wheels
groups.tradeoff: 17" ($1,600–1,900) clears Wilwoods and has the best tire selection. 15" is period-correct but locks you to 11" brakes. 18" ($1,899) is for 14" rotors or a modern stance, with thinner tire choices.

groups.label: Coupe-R look
groups.tradeoff: Scoops, vents, spoiler and canards are all bonded or riveted into the body, so they go on before paint. The hood scoop and footbox vents give most of the look; the splitter and canards are the pieces that scrape and crack on the street.

groups.label: Paint
groups.tradeoff: A shop blocking and painting a coupe runs $8k–20k; doing your own prep can halve it. Title in gelcoat first either way.

groups.label: Insulation
groups.tradeoff: Lizard Skin sprays go on before carpet and are the biggest single comfort gain; butyl mat on footboxes and tunnel is near-universal. Exhaust choice matters more than any of it for noise.

groups.label: Engine mounts
groups.tradeoff: Follows the engine; nothing to decide once the engine is picked.

groups.label: Driveshaft
groups.tradeoff: Length depends on the bellhousing and trans; FFR lists two TKX/IRS shafts, so this is a phone call, not a preference.

warnings.msg: The IRS does not fit pin-drive (knock-off) wheels.
warnings.why: Pin-drive hubs need a narrower track than the IRS and the Gen 3 front spindles give. Jeff Kleiner: "the IRS is not compatible with pin drive width so the only option there is a narrowed solid axle," and the Gen 3 spindles "do not accommodate the narrow pin drive width."
warnings.fix: Stay with bolt-on wheels (FFR Halibrands, Vintage Wheel Works, Forgestar). If you want knock-offs, you need the 3-link with a narrowed axle and Mustang spindles, with worse geometry. Resolve this once your wheel pick is bolt-on.

warnings.msg: PS pump and A/C compressor both hang on the 347's front drive.
warnings.why: BluePrint's standard 347 front drive carries the alternator; the A/C option adds a compressor. A hydraulic PS pump needs its own bracket and pulley position, and nobody has documented all three on the BluePrint drive in a Gen 3.
warnings.fix: Call BluePrint (1-800-483-4263) and ask for the front-drive option with both A/C compressor and PS pump, or switch steering to electric assist (ePowerSteering KIT-26) and skip the pump. Resolve once BluePrint confirms in writing.

warnings.msg: Wilwood 12.88" fronts do not clear 15" wheels.
warnings.why: The 12.88" rotor and Dynapro 6 caliper need a 17" minimum wheel; Wilwood lists 17" minimum for this kit on the Type 65 Coupe.
warnings.fix: Pick 17" or 18" Halibrands, or keep the standard 11" brakes with the 15s.

warnings.msg: 14" rotors do not clear 15" wheels.
warnings.why: A 14" rotor plus caliper needs an 18" or 19" wheel.
warnings.fix: Pick 18" Halibrands or Forgestar 19s, or step down to the 12.88" Wilwoods with 17s.

warnings.msg: 14" rotors probably do not clear 17" wheels.
warnings.why: Ron L. runs this brake on 19s; no Gen 3 build shows it on 17s.
warnings.fix: Confirm with Levy Racing before pairing, or go to 18s.

warnings.msg: 12.88" rear Wilwoods do not clear 15" wheels.
warnings.why: Same rotor and caliper size as the fronts; 17" minimum.
warnings.fix: Pick 17" or 18" wheels, or the IRS 11.65" rear brakes.

warnings.msg: The Coyote is tighter at the footbox than a small-block.
warnings.why: FFR's own FAQ says the small-block is the better choice for footroom; the Coyote's width pushes the footbox walls in.
warnings.fix: Sit in a Coyote coupe before ordering if you're over 6 feet. Resolve once you've checked.

warnings.msg: Kirkeys on a seat track cost you headroom.
warnings.why: Tall drivers floor-mount Kirkeys to gain 1–1.5" of headroom; a track puts it back.
warnings.fix: Skip the track (12077) with Kirkeys, or keep the track with FFR seats. Resolve if you've sat in the car and it fits.
warnings.src: Will I physically fit in a Type 65

warnings.msg: The Tilton bearing duplicates the one in the BluePrint package.
warnings.why: BluePrint's 347/TKX package ships with a McLeod hydraulic throw-out bearing; FFR's 34158 master kit is all you need.
warnings.fix: Drop the Tilton bearing unless you're not using the BluePrint package.

warnings.msg: The Coupe-R is a competition chassis: a cage you sit next to without a helmet, 750/500 lb springs, and a fixed race seat.
warnings.why: FFR sells it as an SCCA/NASA wheel-to-wheel chassis. Cage tubes beside an unhelmeted head are a known street hazard even padded; the spring rates are track rates; the high-back seat has no tracks. SMF-Coupe (Coupe-R): the extra cage tubes made the doors "a major pain": he cut and re-welded the door frames and cut the inside of the doors around the tubing.
warnings.fix: A street Coupe-R is doable, but budget for it: SFI roll-bar padding on every tube near a head, softer springs (FFR's street rates are far below 750/500), the low-back seats on tracks instead of the fixed high-back, side windows, and an FFR tech check that the A/C kit clears the cage. Or order the street kit with the Coupe-R aero options and get the look without the list.

warnings.msg: Confirm the A/C evaporator and ducts clear the Coupe-R cage before ordering both.
warnings.why: The street A/C kit was designed around the standard chassis; no documented Coupe-R build runs it.
warnings.fix: Email tech@factoryfive.com with both part numbers; ask for a Coupe-R build with A/C.

warnings.msg: Side windows on a Coupe-R: confirm the door-bar and cage clearance.
warnings.why: The Coupe-R is sold without side windows; the cage door bars sit where the window mechanism lives.
warnings.fix: Ask FFR before ordering; FormaCars has not documented a cage car either.

warnings.msg: The street kit has no cage. Wheel-to-wheel racing needs the Coupe-R chassis; even open track days often require a roll bar.
warnings.why: The Coupe-R's SCCA/NASA-legal cage is welded into the chassis; it can't be added to the street chassis later without a fabricator.
warnings.fix: For a dedicated track car pick the Coupe-R kit. For time trials or HPDE, check the sanctioning body's roll-bar rule before ordering.

warnings.msg: Track days in the street kit: check the roll-bar rule of the groups you'd run with.
warnings.why: Many HPDE organizers accept a closed coupe as-is; some require a bar or a cage for convertibles only. Rules vary by group.
warnings.fix: Ask the local track-day organizer before the kit order; if a bar is needed, a fabricator can add one to the street chassis but it costs more than ordering the Coupe-R.

warnings.msg: A/C on a dedicated track car is weight, belt load and plumbing you don't need.
warnings.why: The compressor, condenser and evaporator add about 40 lb and a belt-driven load; track builds skip it and run a defroster-only heater or nothing.
warnings.fix: Skip the A/C kit, or pick the heater-only path. Keep a defroster if you'll ever drive it in the wet.

warnings.msg: Powered roll-down windows are the wrong spend on a track car.
warnings.why: Weight and complexity in the doors, and most race rules want the windows down or out anyway.
warnings.fix: Run the FFR sliders or no side glass; put the money into brakes or seats.

warnings.msg: Mass-loaded vinyl is pure weight on a track car.
warnings.why: The quiet-cabin stack adds 40–60 lb; it exists to make a street car livable.
warnings.fix: Heat shielding only (Lizard Skin ceramic or header shields), skip the sound layers.

warnings.msg: A 4-point harness is not accepted for wheel-to-wheel and many track days; the kit's Simpson 5-point is.
warnings.why: Most sanctioning bodies require 5- or 6-point with an anti-submarine strap; 4-points are a street compromise.
warnings.fix: Keep the Simpson 5-point for track use, or run both: harness for the track, stock-style belts for the street.

when: Boig Motorsport headers + quiet side pipes
warnings.msg: Quiet pipes on a track car: only if the track has a sound limit.
warnings.why: Boig's pipes exist for cabin noise on the street; on track you wear a helmet and intercom. Many tracks do have a dB limit (Pacific Raceways enforces one), so check.
warnings.fix: Keep them if your home track measures sound; otherwise the FFR or GAS-N pipes save money.

warnings.msg: The fixed high-back race seat has no tracks and tall wings that eat headroom under the roof.
warnings.why: It is bolted for one driver; sharing the car, or a 6'2" driver under the coupe roof, is where builders go back to the low-backs.
warnings.fix: Low-back aluminum seats on tracks keep the look; Kirkeys are the thin-shell alternative.

when: Coupe-R front aero bumper, canards & splitter
warnings.msg: Splitter and canards on a street car: driveways, speed bumps and parking blocks.
warnings.why: The splitter is the lowest point on the car; canards are the first thing to crack. Owners who keep them learn to park nose-out.
warnings.fix: Take the hood scoop, vents and spoiler for the Coupe-R look and leave the front aero off, or plan to live with scrapes.

warnings.msg: 315 rear tires on the 18" Halibrands rub the frame behind the passenger seat on the IRS.
warnings.why: The coupe body is wider than the roadster but the IRS is the same, so the wheels sit inboard. edwardb needed a full 1" Eibach spacer and camber eased to -0.5/-0.75°; Jphoenix and Rsnake notched the frame for 315/335s at race camber.
warnings.fix: Budget a 1" spacer pair (p227) or order wheels with 5.46" backspacing; keep rear camber near -0.5°. Moving the Koni to the other frame hole changes nothing at the same ride height.

warnings.msg: The Snakebite driver footbox extension does not work with a Coyote (edwardb).
warnings.why: The Coyote's width takes the room the extension uses; it was designed around small-block builds.
warnings.fix: On a 347 you are fine. Coyote builders angle the seat and move the Wilwood pedal pads instead.

warnings.msg: GAS-N pipes and headers: fit and delivery are "a roll of the dice" since 2025 (Jeff Kleiner).
warnings.why: PNWTim's side pipes arrived with the mounting tab welded a foot from where 460.465USMC's set has it; his first headers were poorly made; waits ran months after Georgie left. JimStone: the FFR stainless pipes and headers were a "perfect fit, no fuss". On ffcars, Laser Stan measured three sets of GAS-N "quiet" pipes at 119–120 dB, same as the stock FFR pipes.
warnings.fix: Order FFR's headers and pipes (PNWTim: "quite nice now") and quiet them with inserts (p230), or go Boig/Tubular Automotive. If you still want GAS-N, order early and test-fit on arrival; Horacio replaced PNWTim's.

warnings.msg: The 60627 road-race spoiler arrives rough: ragged edge, thick uneven flange, rocks on the body with 0.100–0.125" gaps.
warnings.why: PNWTim's and Jphoenix's were both like that. Jphoenix also notes FFR/John George aero testing found the spoiler adds drag when a wing is fitted; he would leave it off a street car.
warnings.fix: Jeff Kleiner: thin the flange to ~0.090", cut it to 3/4", heat-gun it to the body curve, 8-32 button heads at 4.75" spacing. Or bond it from below through a slot like TwinFins (thread 134552) before paint.

warnings.msg: The Koni DA top-eye snap rings will not seat; four builders fought them 2022–2026.
warnings.why: The ring catches on the radius of the aluminum top eye. Koni engineering says it is not needed with these spring seats.
warnings.fix: Leave the ring off, or fit a stainless spiral retaining ring (p239). Do not hammer it.

warnings.msg: Decide the IRS rear sway bar before assembly: its brackets are captured by the LCA front bolt and the toe-link bolt.
warnings.why: edwardb has installed the FFR IRS bar twice; retrofitting means pulling those bolts with the car together. Several Gen 3 owners end up running front bar only because the rear bar adds snap oversteer.
warnings.fix: Factory Five will not sell the rear brackets alone (tech, Nov 2026): order the front-and-rear kit, fit the brackets at IRS assembly, and start with the front bar only.

decideLabels.body: Decide before the body goes on

deps.why: Panels and hardware have to be inventoried before anything is drilled.
Footbox and floor panels go in before the pedal box and suspension.
Rear panels and trunk floor before the IRS cradle.
Pedal box and clutch hydraulics before the engine goes in.
Driveshaft and IRS before the trans is final.
Harness routes around the engine and headers.
A/C wiring and the firewall corner share space with the harness.
Evaporator and condenser plumbing is far easier with no body.
Drive it first; find the leaks and fit problems before the body hides them.
WSP inspects a complete, drivable car.
Title in gelcoat so the deadline doesn't depend on the paint shop.
Carpet and seats go in after paint; nothing gets scratched twice.
Alignment and corner balance with the car at final weight.

gates.label: Insulate and seal before the body goes on
steps: Install footbox heat shields and firewall insulation
Seal the footbox-to-body gap with dense foam
Spray or lay sound deadening before carpet areas close
gates.why: Once the body is on, the footbox-to-body gap and the firewall corner are unreachable. Every heat-and-noise regret thread on the coupe traces back to skipping this.

gates.label: A/C, heater and wipers plumbed body-off
steps: Mount the evaporator in the passenger footbox
Run bulkhead fittings and hoses (90° for SBF)
Build the defrost path; have lines crimped and charged
gates.why: FFR: wipers and A/C are 'much easier with the body off.'

gates.label: Windows decided
gates.why: FormaCars roll-downs need door-skin work before door finishing; sliders don't. Decide before the doors are hung.

gates.label: Title first
steps: Pass inspection; get the VIN assigned
gates.why: The WSP certificate is valid 60 days; title before the car leaves for paint.

gates.label: Seat fit confirmed
gates.why: Seat drop and pedal placement decide headroom for a 6'2" driver; mount before carpet.

gates.label: Clutch hydraulics in
steps: Mount the pedal box; set pedal height and dead pedal
gates.why: The master cylinder and line route before the engine blocks access.

p105.note: 60371 side windows ship late; often backordered

p061.note: FFR A/C kit ships with the kit if ordered up front; otherwise allow a month

plans.title: Cabin comfort plan
plans.intro: The Gen 3 cabin is hot and loud, and every fix goes in before the body does. Four decisions share that one truth. Pick a target, and the plan tells you whether your combination gets there.

targets.label: Weekend cruiser, can talk at 60
targets.desc: Quiet pipes or inserts, butyl mat, footbox shields.

targets.label: Grand tourer, long drives in the rain
targets.desc: Quiet pipes, full spray insulation + MLV, FFR A/C with a defrost path, roll-down windows.

facts: Stock FFR side pipes measured about 114 dB inside; the exhaust is the dominant noise source, more than any insulation choice.
After extensive insulation a coupe still read above 80 dB at cruise (ffcars Planning thread); insulation lowers the floor, it does not make a quiet car.
Most cockpit heat is engine-bay air pushed along the footbox-to-body gap, not conduction; dense foam at that gap beats another layer of mat.
FFR's evaporator has two always-on outlets and no defrost diverter; builders add Y-connections to defrost and dash outlets. Washington's inspection checks the defroster if installed.
Lizard Skin and mat must go on before carpet, and the footbox-to-body gap is unreachable once the body is on.

rows.label: Exhaust
rows.note: Biggest single lever. Inserts are the cheap fix on either FFR or GAS-N pipes.

rows.label: Insulation
rows.note: Spray goes on first, then mat, then MLV under the carpet. Pick more than one.

rows.label: A/C and heat
rows.note: FFR's kit fits; plan the defrost Y-connections. FormaCars is the better-defrost route.

rows.label: Windows
rows.note: Sliders leak a little and seal poorly; roll-downs are the wet-climate answer.

plans.title: Driver fit plan (6'2")
plans.intro: Headroom and legroom in a Gen 3 come from five choices that interact. The rear brace limits seat travel, so the seat choice does most of the work.

targets.label: Fits, helmet optional
targets.desc: Stock-style seat on tracks and a 14" wheel. Comfortable to about 6'0"; a helmet is tight.

targets.label: Fits at 6'2" with a helmet
targets.desc: Thin-shell seat on the floor, small wheel, quick release.

facts: Floor-mounting the seat instead of using the track gains 1 to 1.5 inches of headroom.
FFR's low-back aluminum seats are the ones FFR itself markets for tall drivers; Kirkey's shell is thinner still.
A 13-inch wheel adds knee room; a quick-release hub adds entry room, which matters more in a coupe.
One builder could not make a Corbeau fit the driver's side at all and went back to FFR seats.
Sit in a finished coupe before buying seats; Fredscoupe in Everett offered.

plans.title: Washington rain plan
plans.intro: Nobody has documented a fully weather-tight Gen 3 coupe. How dry and how safe it is in the wet comes down to the windows, the wipers, the defrost path and what you do about the bare steel.

targets.label: Dry days only
targets.desc: Sliders, stock wipers, garage-kept. Fine for summer cruises.

targets.label: Caught in the rain, no drama
targets.desc: Wipers that clear the big windshield, a real defrost path, bulb seals on the doors, coated pipes.

targets.label: Driven in November anyway
targets.desc: Roll-down windows, sealed marine wipers, LED lighting, a rear camera, coated chassis and exhaust.

rows.label: Side windows
rows.note: Sliders leak a little and seal poorly; roll-downs are the wet-climate answer and the only part here you can't add after paint.

rows.label: Wipers
rows.note: FFR's kit is 'OK but marginal' on the coupe's windshield. Marine motors are sealed to IP66.

rows.label: Defrost
rows.note: A fogged windshield is the real rain problem. FFR's kit has two always-on outlets and no diverter; plan the Y-connections or go FormaCars.

extras: Breeze LED headlight and exterior kits
facts: wallace18 stayed dry through two rainstorms with the FFR windows plus added foam and reworked frames, but says it won't match a production car.
Wayne Yoshida (Gen 1 coupe) skipped ceramic coating and the bare pipes rusted in a year.
edwardb runs the Specialty Power Windows wiper kit; builders call the FFR wipers marginal on the big windshield.
The hatch glass heat-soaks the cabin in sun and fogs in rain; tint it and give the defrost a path to it.
Seal the footbox-to-body gap and every panel seam with Sikaflex before the body goes on; water finds the same gaps the heat does.
The coupe's rear blind spot is real; a camera mirror is the common fix and matters more in the wet.
